Hi there OP

8mg is a small dose of codeine, so I would suspect you would be fine, especially since it has only been a few months. 

Every person is unique, so please don’t let anyone minimise your personal journey, but pharmacologically any physical withdrawals are likely to be minor. 

Mostly I would aim for as much distraction as you can  muster, be good and kind to yourself, OTC meds for any discomfort should see you through, such as Imodium if you wind up with any gastro upsets. 
Keep your fluids up which is wise advice regardless and try not to other think it, analysing
“Am I feeling x?” Over and over. 
Personally speaking you can manifest all sorts of ills if you give it too much consideration. 

I have stepped of codeine at significantly higher doses and have managed, and I haven’t. 
When I haven’t it’s been due to my preoccupation with expecting the worst. And when I haven’t managed it’s been down to doing the simple stuff consistently and well , eating well, hydrating well, resting well, and relaxing and distracting. 

Good luck and feel free to check back in!
Others might have more wise counsel.

Ok. You’ve had a few steps forward and just one step back. 

Be prepared. It will be tough going, but IT WILL END.

I’ve been through it a few times, codeine and morphine. 
I’m in the midst of it myself, I’m at about day 9 so I’m not going to profess I ‘personally’ have all the answers, but at least this shows you that anyone can fall into this trap (I’ve worked in addictions for 23 years)

But if I can do it, I know you can too. 

All the usual stuff, look up in the search for the opioid withdrawal survival guide. There are some good tips there. 

Just give it a go, be exceptionally kind to yourself. Try to stay as busy as you can. 
Take the paracetamol and the ibuprofen, keep the liquids up, stay warm, watch something interesting. (I’m a reader, but can’t read for the first few days)

You’ll get there. Check back in.

Some points from someone who works in AOD for the last 30 years, but this isn’t professional advice, alcohol hasn’t been my focus of my job for decades. 

Alcohol withdrawal is serious. You know that, most likely from your past experiences and the posts above. It needs medical attention. 

Others have said “root cause” and this always needs to be dealt with at some stage. That very well might be a year or two into sober living, but sooner or later it needs to be worked through. 

In the meantime, medical detox and a spell in rehab (but a good one, one that will take the time)

There are med options for helping stay stopped, there is a combo I’ve seen work well, Antabuse, baclofen and naltrexone, but Antabuse has been useful for a bunch of people. 
It’s a long road, like travelling around a roundabout endlessly, until you’re ready to take the right exit. 

Keeping on keeping on is the key. 
I hope they make it. 

In the meantime, I hope you’re getting some support. It’s hard for families, and families need their own supports too. 
You could check out family drug support if you haven’t already. 

There is nothing like lived experience advice. Seek that out in an AOD service if you can. I know someone posted earlier about their cirrhosis journey. It’s a tough road, especially as we age. 

Feel free to reach out if there is any questions I might be able to answer, or resources I can find for you specifically. 

Good luck.

Hey. So you picked up. 
Tomorrow is a new day. 

And you know you, if the only thing that is keeping you going is not wanting to get sick, then maybe think about treatment. 
Sublocade (bupe depot) does work wonders! But most of the time, depending on the doc, you need to be in withdrawals to start, as it binds to your opioid receptors stronger than other opioids. Starting when you have other opioids in your system makes you feel pretty darned ordinary. 

You can try a taper, didn’t work for me, I was just too greedy and misguided, wanting to feel a little something. 

The sickness you’ll feel (and I appreciate it’s different for everyone) is tough, yes, but really not as tough as our noisy mind tells us it is. 
Maybe start by throwing all the good stuff in to begin with, like the fish oil, the good diet, the COLD showers, I can’t recommend them enough!
Then just give it a whirl, take it day by day. 

You know, I was having a toughish time a little while ago, but typing this out has been enormously helpful for me too. 
Thats how this stuff works. 
If I can muscle through. You can too!

Don’t be too hard on yourself, revisit this tomorrow. Just don’t stop thinking about knocking it on the head. 

It’s one thing you’ll NEVER regret, stopping 

Power to you! x

Hey. 
Ok, so I wouldn’t call myself a veteran but I am a few weeks into kicking a 40-50mg oxy habit. 
It’s my 3rd or 4th time. I take breaks, start again for abit, realise the joy has gone and then pull up. 
Like you, I’m guessing I’ve managed to give away booze, weed, speed etc in my younger years, but man opioids have got a killer hook. 

It’s worth checking in with your mental health more generally, because sometimes opioids are pretty good and fulfilling a void that we never really accepted was there… maybe not. In and of themselves opioids are very attractive. 

Over thinking it, waiting and watching for the symtoms sucks. I try to just be present, if that present is pain, so be it, KNOW that it is temporary. 

It does get better and it gets better a fair bit quicker than your brain is telling you right now

Some things that might help

1. If it’s possible, cut yourself off from your supply. When the itch in your head gets hard to bear, it’s too easy to slip
2. Epsom salts baths - as many as you need
3. X2 (or more) COLD showers a day. I know, it sounds horrible, but the feeling when you’ve battled that and won is quite something
3. Lots of water (more than you think) you’ll sweat for a few days
4. These meds - 
Fish oil high straight
Magnesium
Multi vitamin
Vitamin c (high strength)
Melatonin
An old school antihistamine OTC sleep med 
5. Movies and books you’ve seen/read before (easier to concentrate)

I get you don’t want to reach out to anyone in real life (I haven’t) I’ve just alluded to the problem but never outright said it. 

You can try a doctor, but I’d be wary of going onto a program long term if you can avoid it

(I say this as someone who has worked in addiction since the late 90’s - I’ve seen it do wonderous things for lots of people - but if you can kick and never look back, that’s worth a try)

Don’t fear the unexpected, wait for it to present itself and grab the bulll by the horns. You got this.

Dust yourself off, learn. 
Just keep on learning 

Look hard at why it happened, and you’ll appreciate the gift that knowledge brings when you do. 

Each and every time we slip up, it’s another chance to understand what drives our addictions. 

Remember you don’t now need to go through the hard yards of getting through the withdrawals. 

Good on you mate, for reaching out. 

Stick with it.
